summary: This standards-track document describes elliptic curve key exchange algorithms for TLS, in particular ephemeral ECDH key agreement and the use of ECDSA in the handshake, for TLS 1.2 and earlier. It was later replaced by RFC 9846.

eli5.summary: A way for a website and your browser to agree on a secret using clever curve math. It was later replaced by RFC 9846.

questions: how does tls use elliptic curve cryptography
subtitle: How TLS 1.2 and earlier use elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curve signatures in the handshake.

tldr.problem: TLS needs a way to agree on a shared secret and to authenticate the peers, and elliptic curves offer this with smaller keys than older methods.
tldr.mechanism: Server and client each use an ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key to compute the premaster secret. ECDSA, EdDSA or RSA signatures authenticate the server, and two TLS extensions let the client say which curves and point formats it supports.
tldr.outcome: It defines the ECC cipher suites and curves for TLS 1.2 and earlier, and adds x25519 and x448. It obsoletes RFC 4492 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9846.

today: RFC 8422 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9846. It was also updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015. It replaced RFC 4492.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 8422 describes additions to TLS to support Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) in TLS versions 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2. The use of ECC in TLS 1.3 is defined elsewhere and is explicitly out of scope. The document defines two things: the use of the ECDHE key agreement scheme with ephemeral keys to establish the TLS premaster secret, and the use of ECDSA and EdDSA signatures to authenticate TLS peers.

It obsoletes RFC 4492. Most of its text comes from that predecessor, but it removes a lot of old options, as the changes section below explains.
sections.eli5: This memo says how websites and browsers can use curve-shaped math to make a shared secret and prove who they are. It only covers the older versions of TLS.

sections.title: Key Exchange Algorithms
sections.content:
Three key exchange algorithms are defined. All of them use ephemeral ECDH (ECDHE) to compute the TLS premaster secret and differ only in how, or whether, they authenticate. The later steps that derive the master secret and bulk encryption keys are unchanged by ECC.

  • ECDHE_ECDSA: the server certificate MUST hold an ECDSA- or EdDSA-capable key, and the ephemeral parameters in the ServerKeyExchange message are signed with it.
  • ECDHE_RSA: the same, except the certificate holds an RSA key and the signature is made with the RSA private key. The server can reuse an existing RSA certificate, at a higher computational cost than the traditional RSA key exchange, which gives no forward secrecy.
  • ECDH_anon: the parameters are not signed and the Certificate, CertificateRequest and CertificateVerify messages are not sent. It is open to man-in-the-middle attacks, so applications SHOULD authenticate by other means.

All three provide forward secrecy if and only if fresh ephemeral keys are generated and destroyed after use. The server sends its ephemeral public key and the curve in the ServerKeyExchange message, and the client replies with its own public key in ClientKeyExchange. The shared secret becomes the premaster secret.

For client authentication, the one mechanism is ECDSA_sign, where the client holds a certificate with an ECDSA- or EdDSA-capable key and proves possession by signing in CertificateVerify. A client certificate may be of a different type than the server certificate.
sections.eli5: Both sides make up a temporary secret number and swap clues made from it. A website can also sign its clue to prove it is the real site, but the anonymous version skips the proof and is easier to trick.

sections.title: Negotiating Curves and Point Formats
sections.content:
Two TLS extensions let the client and server agree on what they can handle: the Supported Elliptic Curves extension (elliptic_curves, type 10) and the Supported Point Formats extension (ec_point_formats, type 11). A client that offers ECC cipher suites SHOULD include them, and a client that offers none MUST NOT. Servers MUST NOT negotiate an ECC cipher suite unless they can finish the handshake using the client's chosen curves.

The curve list is ordered by the client's preference. This document keeps three NIST curves, secp256r1 (23), secp384r1 (24) and secp521r1 (25), and adds x25519 (29) and x448 (30). It deprecates the other curves from RFC 4492 (numbers 1 to 22) and explicit curves. For point formats, only uncompressed (0) remains, and a list that is sent MUST include it. If a client sends the extension without it and offers a curve from this document, the server MUST abort with an illegal_parameter alert.

For signatures, EdDSA hashes data internally, so the RFC adds a dummy hash value called Intrinsic (8). The values (8,7) and (8,8) represent ed25519 and ed448 in the signature_algorithms extension. On session resumption the server ignores both ECC extensions.
sections.eli5: Before swapping secrets, the browser tells the website which kinds of curves it understands, favorite first. The website must pick something from that list, or skip the curve method entirely.

sections.title: Handshake Messages and Computations
sections.content:
The ServerKeyExchange message carries ServerECDHParams: the curve parameters and the server's ephemeral public key as an ECPoint. The only remaining curve type is named_curve (3). The signature covers the ClientHello random, the ServerHello random and the parameters. ECDSA signatures are DER-encoded pairs of integers r and s, while EdDSA signs the raw data and follows RFC 8032.

For the NIST curves, points use the uncompressed form: one form octet, then the X and Y values in big-endian. For P-256 each coordinate takes 32 octets, for P-384 it takes 48 and for P-521 it takes 66. For X25519 and X448 the public value is a 32- or 56-octet representation.

ECDH on the NIST curves uses the ECKAS-DH1 scheme from IEEE 1363, and the premaster secret is the x-coordinate of the shared point with leading zeros kept. With X25519 the premaster secret is exactly 32 bytes, and with X448 it is 56 bytes. If either party gets an all-zero shared secret it MUST abort the handshake.

The CertificateRequest type ecdsa_sign has value 64. Certificates that carry ECC keys MUST follow RFC 3279, or RFC 8410 for EdDSA. The RFC lists ECC cipher suites such as TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (0xC0, 0x2F), and says servers SHOULD support four of them: the ECDHE_RSA and ECDHE_ECDSA suites with AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and with AES_128_CBC_SHA.
sections.eli5: The website sends its curve and its public clue, with a signature to prove it is real. The browser sends back its own clue, and both do the same math to get the same secret.

sections.title: Security Notes and Changes from RFC 4492
sections.content:
With the NIST curves, each party MUST check that the peer's public key satisfies the curve equation. Skipping this lets attackers learn about the private key, and they may recover the whole key in a few requests if it is not really ephemeral. For X25519 and X448 the check is that the shared secret is not all zeros.

The security section says all key exchanges defined here provide forward secrecy, and that curve choice matters: less algebraic structure is the more conservative option, and a single widely used curve risks a catastrophic failure if it is attacked. It points to RFC 8032 for the advantages of EdDSA over ECDSA with the NIST curves.

Compared with RFC 4492, this document adds TLS 1.2 and X25519 and X448, merges errata, removes the ECDH_RSA and ECDH_ECDSA key exchanges, deprecates a number of cipher suites including RC4 suites, drops unused curves, explicit curves and all but the uncompressed point format, and lifts the restriction that matched the certificate signature algorithm.
sections.eli5: A good browser double-checks the other side's clue to make sure it is a real, safe one. This memo also cleans out old, risky choices from the first version.
